planting.note: Best grown in a container in a gritty, fast-draining mineral mix except in the mildest, driest climates.

directions: Grow in extremely well-drained, lean, mineral-heavy soil in full sun to very bright light, keeping the compact rosette dry through winter. Native to dry limestone slopes near Oaxaca, Mexico, this small, solitary species carries thick, chalky-white to pale gray-green leaves armed with bold, dark chocolate-brown teeth and terminal spines that stand out dramatically against the pale leaf surface. It grows slowly and stays compact for years, making it a favorite specimen for pots and rock gardens rather than open-ground xeriscapes in most of the country. Protect from prolonged freezing and from overhead water, since rot is the main threat to this desert species outside its native range.
sources: Agave: Living Sculptures for Landscapes and Containers (Timber Press)

planting.note: Plant in a raised, gravel-mulched bed for best cold and wet-winter survival.

directions: Plant in sharply drained, gritty soil in full sun; this Coahuila, Mexico native forms a dense, tightly packed rosette of broad, powdery silver-blue leaves that curl inward like cupped cabbage leaves, each tipped with a long, near-black terminal spine and reddish marginal teeth. It tolerates more cold and moisture than many single-rosette agaves and is one of the hardier choices for a striking blue accent in raised xeriscape beds. Older rosettes eventually offset sparingly, so plan on division rather than rapid clumping for propagation. Give it excellent drainage in winter to avoid basal rot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Site where the curling marginal threads catch backlight for best display.

directions: Grow in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun to light shade; this old-in-cultivation Mexican species forms a tight, symmetrical rosette of narrow, dark green leaves edged with fine white filaments that peel and curl away from the leaf margin, giving the whole plant a shaggy, thread-wrapped look year-round. It stays compact and offsets modestly to form small colonies over time, making it a reliable small-scale accent for gravel gardens, pots, and border edges. It is more forgiving of light shade and irregular water than many larger agave species. Remove old lower leaves as they brown to keep the rosette tidy.
sources: Agave: Living Sculptures for Landscapes and Containers (Timber Press)

planting.note: Give afternoon shade in hottest, driest climates to keep variegation from scorching.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun near the coast or partial shade inland; this variegated sport of foxtail agave carries crisp cream to white longitudinal stripes running the length of its broad, spineless, softly arching leaves, giving the rosette a brighter, more luminous look than the plain species. It is spineless and safe near walkways, but slightly more cold-tender than the species form and should be moved under cover or into a protected microclimate below the low 20s Fahrenheit. Offsets forming at the base can be removed and rooted to increase stock, though variegation can occasionally revert on some pups. Keep water light and infrequent once established.

planting.note: Choose a spot with reflected warmth if gardening near the cold edge of its range.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this selection of foxtail agave was chosen for its consistently powdery, chalky blue-gray leaf color, a cooler and more silvery cast than the soft apple-green of the standard species. Like other foxtail agaves it is spineless and forms a broad, arching, trunk-topping rosette that suckers freely to form handsome clumps over time. It shares the species' relative cold tenderness, so protect it or grow it in a container where winter temperatures regularly drop into the mid-20s Fahrenheit or below. Divide and replant offsets in spring to expand plantings.

planting.note: Excellent low-water accent for slopes and mass plantings where its symmetry can be appreciated from above.

directions: Plant in fast-draining, lean soil in full sun; this hybrid between foxtail agave and Agave shawii was bred for an intensely blue, almost metallic leaf color combined with a neat, symmetrical, nearly spineless rosette that holds its shape year-round. It is markedly more sun- and cold-tolerant than pure foxtail agave, taking brief dips into the mid-20s Fahrenheit without significant damage, while retaining the smooth, safe-to-brush-past leaf margins that make attenuata hybrids popular near walkways and pools. Growth is slow to moderate, and mature rosettes offset sparingly at the base. Avoid overhead irrigation and winter wet to keep the rosette tight and rot-free.

planting.note: Grow in a container or protected bed outside the mildest zones, since it is among the more cold-sensitive trunking yuccas.

directions: Plant in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; this slow-growing Mexican species forms an eventually trunking rosette of narrow, softly arching leaves that shift from blue-green through dusky purple to near-plum depending on light intensity and season, with the deepest color developing under bright, stressful sun exposure. It stays smaller and slower than most trunk-forming yuccas, making it a good specimen for large containers as well as protected ground beds. It is less cold-hardy than the widespread American Yucca species and benefits from a warm, sheltered site or winter protection outside the mildest zones. Allow the soil to dry fully between waterings.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow in a pot that can be moved under cover in winter outside the mildest coastal climates.

directions: Grow in well-drained soil in bright light to gentle morning sun, giving afternoon shade in hot inland climates to prevent leaf scorch. This branching, shrubby sport of Aeonium decorum carries small rosettes edged in a shifting band of pink and cream that deepens to rosy blush in cool weather and bright light, framing a soft green leaf center. It stays compact and multi-headed, quickly filling containers or the front of a succulent bed with color, and roots readily from stem cuttings taken from any healthy branch. Like other Aeoniums it rests and may drop lower leaves in hot, dry summer conditions, resuming active growth with cooler, wetter fall and winter weather. Protect from frost and from prolonged summer drought stress, both of which can weaken or kill rosettes.
